analysis.one_liner: Pauses most debt collection—lawsuits, repossessions, credit damage, garnishments—during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency and for 120 days after it ends, the bill would have stopped debt collectors and creditors from adding penalty interest or fees, suing over past-due debt, repossessing cars or foreclosing on homes, reporting missed payments to credit bureaus, garnishing wages, or seizing bank accounts. It also would have kept utilities and phone or internet service from being shut off for nonpayment, and banned 'confessions of judgment'—signed waivers that let a lender win a court judgment against a borrower without notice or a hearing. Missed payments would have been tacked onto the end of the loan instead of triggering penalties. The bill was introduced in the House on March 31, 2020, sent to the Financial Services Committee, and never moved again [S1][S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households, small businesses, and nonprofits that fell behind on debts during the pandemic would have gotten breathing room: no new penalty fees or interest, no lawsuits or threatened suits, no repossessions or foreclosures, no wage or bank-account garnishment (child and spousal support excepted), no negative credit reporting, and no utility or broadband shutoffs. Missed payments would have been rescheduled rather than defaulted [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, small businesses, and nonprofits behind on debts

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars debt collectors and creditors from adding extra interest or fees triggered by nonpayment, suing or threatening to sue, continuing existing collection lawsuits, repossessing property, or foreclosing during the emergency period plus 120 days [S2][S3].

It stops collection through wage garnishment, benefit offset, or seizure of bank accounts, and blocks banks from exercising a 'right of set off'—taking money straight out of a borrower's account to cover a debt [S2][S3].
It forbids reporting past-due debt to credit bureaus, so people who missed payments during the emergency would not carry the damage on their credit records [S2][S3].
It prevents shutoff of electricity, natural gas, telecommunications, broadband, water, or sewer service during the covered period [S2][S3].

It bans confessions of judgment—agreements in which a borrower waives notice and the chance to be heard in court before a lender can obtain a judgment—and requires that missed payments be added back onto the end of the payment schedule after the emergency [S2][S3].
Violators would be liable for ten times the damages available under the existing Fair Debt Collection Practices Act enforcement provision [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Creditors, debt collectors, banks (which could no longer seize account funds), credit reporting agencies (which would lose the flow of delinquency data), and utilities and telecom companies (which could not disconnect service for nonpayment) would have absorbed the cost of unpaid obligations during the covered period. Debts were not forgiven—payments would be rescheduled—so lenders would wait rather than write anything off [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Creditors and some economists argue a blanket moratorium can backfire: lenders respond to not being able to collect by tightening credit or raising rates for everyone afterward, and the bill does not forgive debts, only delays them, so borrowers emerge owing the same amounts [S3].

The bill was written to apply to any debt, including debts owed to federal, state, and local governments, and to cover litigation already underway, raising questions about how courts and agencies would unwind cases mid-stream during a 120-day window [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households and small businesses facing sudden income loss in spring 2020, a pause on lawsuits, repossessions, garnishments, utility shutoffs, and credit damage would have provided real, immediate relief, and the rescheduling mechanism means the debts were deferred rather than erased. The main cost falls on lenders and collectors, who would wait longer to be paid and might restrict credit later. The bill never advanced far enough to be refined, so design questions—like how already-filed lawsuits would be handled—were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Al Lawson introduced the bill on March 31, 2020, about three weeks after the national COVID-19 emergency was declared, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S3][S5].
Three Democratic colleagues signed on as cosponsors [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup, the bill never reached the House floor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the bill still pending in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collectors, creditors, and banks were better off because the moratorium never became law; households that lost income during the pandemic got no federal pause on collections, garnishments, repossessions, or credit reporting.

for.name: Rep. Al Lawson, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Rep. Maxine Waters, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; it remained pending in committee through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill (a representative and three cosponsors), and no Republican supported it on record, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one had to take a public position on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from suing, repossessing, garnishing, or adding penalty fees during the emergency, delaying payment on outstanding debts. Their interest in collecting on schedule ran directly against borrowers' need for relief during a pandemic income shock [S2][S3].
Banks could not have exercised their right to seize funds directly from a borrower's account to cover a debt, and would have held loans with missed payments for longer [S3].
The bill bans reporting past-due debt during the covered period, cutting off new delinquency data that feeds credit scores [S2][S3].
They could not disconnect electricity, gas, water, phone, or broadband service for nonpayment during the covered period, bearing unpaid-bill costs while households kept service [S3].
